name: Resume design
routing_text: How should a software engineer or data scientist write their resume? Bullet points, professional summary, page length, formatting and layout, ATS keyword matching, quantified impact and metrics, tailoring a CV to one job description, and what a recruiter looks for in the seconds they spend skimming it.
blurb: What a technical resume has to do on the page before anyone reads it closely.

units.summary: Recruiters are looking for agentic systems experience, not generic terms like semantic queries. A resume with typos will not have its projects checked by recruiters. Referrals are the social proof that tells recruiters you have worked with former colleagues. Hiring managers care about the impact you made, not just your responsibilities.

units.summary: The job market is tough for software engineers, so resumes must be on point. An AI engineer requires AI, LLM, NLP, Python (preferred), C, and Java. For an AI engineer resume, projects should highlight LLMs, APIs, embeddings and the latest tools like LangChain. You must take ownership of ambiguous problems and drive them from ideation to solution without waiting for instructions.

units.summary: The featured section can make a positive impression on recruiters. You can add links to your portfolio website, app, open source contribution, article, LinkedIn post, or any other achievement in the featured section. Leveraging your feature section makes a positive impression on recruiters. The better and more often you have those keywords spread through your profile, the easier it is for LinkedIn to push you in search results.

units.title: resume formula, project section, measurable impact, entry-level engineer, action verb, professional experience
units.summary: Hiring managers care about the impact you made, not just your responsibilities. The Resume Formula can be used to write a winning resume. For entry-level engineers, education should come at the top of the resume. For experienced hires, skill, project, and education sections should be placed at the bottom of the resume, not the top.

rubrics.criterion: Substantiate at least 75% of the job's required skills in experience or project bullets, not only in a skills section.
rubrics.check: Compare the required skills from the job posting against the resume; fail if 25% or more of those required skills appear only in the skills section or not at all in the experience/project bullets.
rubrics.why: Recruiters hunt for qualifications, not keyword lists, so skills that only sit in a section read as keywords and do not prove the applicant can do the job.
rubrics.unit_title: resume, LinkedIn profile, recruiters, linkedin, keywords, ATS

rubrics.criterion: Write every experience bullet as a demonstrated result instead of a vague list of duties.
rubrics.check: Look at each bullet under experience and check whether it names a concrete outcome or impact such as a percentage, a cost, a timeline, or a delivered system; fail if the bullet only describes responsibilities in general terms.
rubrics.why: Vague, task-only bullets make the resume feel risky and get it rejected, while result bullets show the reader you have already done the job and can do it again.
rubrics.unit_title: resume, LinkedIn profile, recruiters, linkedin, keywords, ATS

rubrics.criterion: Keep the resume to exactly one page.
rubrics.check: Open the rendered resume and count the pages; fail if the content extends beyond page one.
rubrics.why: Recruiters spend an average of 7 seconds per resume, so anything beyond one page is unlikely to be read and can get the applicant passed over.

rubrics.criterion: Put the required technical skills for the target role inside your experience and project bullets, not only in a skill section.
rubrics.check: For an AI/ML engineer resume, take the required technology list (AI, LLM, NLP, Python, ML frameworks, cloud, APIs, etc.) and scan the Experience/Projects sections. Pass if at least 75% of those skills appear in bullet context and no core AI skill appears only as a standalone label.
rubrics.why: Recruiters hunt for qualifications, not keywords; a resume that claims an AI role but shows no AI in the actual work gets rejected in seconds.

rubrics.criterion: Quantify the result in each experience or project bullet with a concrete number, metric, percentage, or duration.
rubrics.check: Scan every bullet under Experience and Projects. If a bullet claims an outcome (built, improved, led, achieved) without any numeric metric attached, mark it as a miss; pass only when all outcome bullets carry a specific measure.
rubrics.why: Numbers show that you know the details of your work, and metrics like an F1 score or success rate make your impact intuitive to the recruiter.

rubrics.criterion: Link every serious project to a public, professional artifact such as GitHub, a blog post, or a personal website, and keep that artifact clean and secure.
rubrics.check: Click each link in the resume. For each GitHub repo, verify it has a README, a requirements.txt file, clean code folders, and no public .env file or API keys; fail the resume if any link is broken, the repo is empty, or a secret is exposed.
rubrics.why: Industry professionals use GitHub only, and exposed secrets or messy repos make a recruiter distrust the candidate with production data.

rubrics.criterion: Start every experience bullet with a strong action verb and make the bullet show the business result, not just a responsibility.

rubrics.why: Each bullet should round out the story of how what you did helped the company succeed; otherwise the bullet reads as a duty and loses interview interest.

rubrics.why: Inconsistent spacing makes the resume look unprofessional, and blank space is space that could carry real information.

rubrics.criterion: Keep the Professional Experience section limited to paid work; put volunteer, academic, and personal projects elsewhere.

rubrics.criterion: Order resume sections according to career stage: recent grads and entry-level candidates put education at the top; experienced candidates lead with experience and move skills, projects, and education below it.
rubrics.check: If the author is a recent grad or entry-level candidate, fail if Education is not one of the first sections. If the author has eight-plus years of experience, fail if Skills, Projects, or Education appears before Experience.
rubrics.why: Recruiters use the top sections to decide whether to consider you at that career level; entry-level and experienced rules are completely different.
